analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from vetoing mining waste disposal permits in streams and waterways.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever reaching a vote in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite a section of the Clean Water Act that gives the EPA the power to block permits allowing mining and other industries to dump dredged or fill material into streams and wetlands. It would strip the EPA's ability to veto an already-issued permit, put strict deadlines that would eliminate the EPA's veto power if missed, and require state agencies to consent before federal regulators could give a permit extra scrutiny. It was introduced in March 2011, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and other industries that discharge fill material into waterways gain from reduced EPA oversight of dumping permits, particularly those seeking to dispose of mine waste in streams.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal companies and mining waste permit applicants

how_it_helps.text: It removes the EPA's authority to disapprove a dumping site specification once the Army Corps has issued the permit, and cuts off the EPA entirely if it misses 30- and 60-day review deadlines [S2][S3].
It would allow the Secretary of the Army to reissue, as final action, specifications the EPA had disapproved before the bill's enactment, overriding past EPA vetoes [S2][S3].
It limits EPA's ability to request elevated review of a permit by capping such requests at one per permit and requiring consent from state agencies first [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities that depend on clean water and municipal supplies downstream of permitted dumping sites, and the public, which would lose a legal check on the destruction of streams and wetlands.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream communities and clean water resources

drawbacks.text: The bill removes an EPA check that can block dumping shown to have unacceptable adverse effects on municipal water supplies, shellfish beds and fisheries, wildlife, and recreation areas [S3].
Once a permit was issued or deadlines lapsed, no federal veto could reverse it even if harmful effects were discovered later, leaving affected communities no administrative remedy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to permit applicants was speed and certainty; the cost was removing the only federal mechanism that can stop disposal sites that threaten water supplies, fisheries, and wildlife, with no reversal possible once a permit was issued or a deadline missed.

outcome.mechanism: It never made it past a subcommittee referral in the House and was never brought to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced and referred to committee on March 8, 2011 [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where no further action was taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the EPA's Clean Water Act veto authority remained intact through the end of the 112th Congress, so coal and mining companies did not gain the expanded permitting certainty the bill would have given them.

for.name: Harold Rogers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House [S1][S5].

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referring it to a subcommittee, so it never reached a floor vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and no vote ever occurred [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have removed an EPA veto over permits to dump mining waste into streams and waterways, making disposal permits easier to obtain and shield them from later reversal [S2][S3].
Any industry discharging fill into wetlands or waterways benefits from restricted EPA disapproval and shorter, lapse-based review timelines [S2].
